findings.title: Oklahoma Governor Signs Comprehensive Consumer Data Privacy Law (SB 546)
findings.summary: Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt signed SB 546 on March 20, 2026, making Oklahoma the 20th state to enact a comprehensive consumer data privacy law. The law grants Oklahomans rights to access, correct, delete, and obtain copies of their personal data, as well as opt out of the sale of personal data and certain targeted advertising practices. The law applies to businesses processing personal data of over 100,000 consumers or 25,000 consumers while earning a majority of revenue from data sales. SB 546 takes effect January 1, 2027, with enforcement by the Oklahoma Attorney General following a 30-day cure notice.

findings.title: Kentucky HB 692: First State to Classify Smart TV Automatic Content Recognition Data as Sensitive
findings.summary: Kentucky's HB 692 amends the Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act to define and classify automatic content recognition (ACR) data — screenshots taken every 500 milliseconds by smart TVs to identify viewed content — as sensitive personal data requiring explicit consumer consent before processing. The bill unanimously passed the Kentucky House on March 16, 2026, passed the full legislature, and was delivered to the governor. Kentucky becomes the first state to specifically target smart TV surveillance through a consumer data privacy framework. The bill has an effective date of July 1, 2027.

findings.title: Nebraska Passes Conversational AI Safety Act (LB 525) Requiring Chatbot Disclosure
findings.summary: Nebraska's unicameral legislature passed LB 525, which combines the Agricultural Data Privacy Act and the Conversational AI Safety Act. The chatbot provisions require operators of conversational AI services to disclose to users that the service is not human when a reasonable person would not otherwise understand this, and require disclosure to minors that they are interacting with AI. The bill also prohibits conversational AI services from claiming to provide professional mental or behavioral health care services. This represents one of the first state-level laws specifically targeting chatbot safety and disclosure requirements.

findings.title: White House Releases National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence with Federal Preemption Recommendations
findings.summary: On March 20, 2026, the White House released its National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence, providing legislative recommendations to Congress for establishing a unified federal approach to AI regulation. The Framework is non-binding but recommends that Congress preempt state AI laws inconsistent with the federal policy, adopting a light-touch regulatory approach focused on innovation. Key policy areas include child safety, consumer protection, intellectual property, free speech, and workforce development. The Framework reflects President Trump's December 2025 executive order directing the DOJ to challenge state AI laws through litigation and conditioning federal broadband funding on repeal of state AI regulations.

findings.title: Trump Executive Order Directs Federal Preemption Strategy Against State AI Laws
findings.summary: On December 11, 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order titled 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,' directing the DOJ to establish an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws deemed inconsistent with federal policy, the FTC to issue a policy statement on how the FTC Act applies to AI, and the Department of Commerce to condition $42 billion in broadband funding on repeal of onerous state AI regulations. The EO targets what the administration calls a 'patchwork of onerous and excessive state requirements,' explicitly naming Colorado's AI Act. The EO itself cannot preempt state laws — that requires an act of Congress or court ruling — so state AI laws remain in effect pending legal challenges.

findings.title: California AG Announces Record $2.75 Million CCPA Settlement with Disney
findings.source: California Department of Justice / Troutman Pepper Locke
findings.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a $2.75 million settlement with The Walt Disney Company and ABC on February 11, 2026, the largest CCPA settlement to date. The investigation found Disney failed to honor consumers' opt-out requests across all devices linked to a consumer's Disney account when it came to targeted advertising, despite linking those same devices for ad targeting purposes. Disney's streaming TV apps also lacked a direct opt-out mechanism, redirecting users to a website instead. The settlement includes corrective measures requiring Disney to implement compliant opt-out processes.

findings.title: California Privacy Protection Agency Issues $1.1 Million Fine Against PlayOn Sports for CCPA Violations
findings.summary: On March 3, 2026, the California Privacy Protection Agency Board issued a decision requiring PlayOn Sports to pay a $1.10 million fine and change its business practices after the Agency's Enforcement Division reached a settlement. The action is the CPPA's first enforcement decision addressing privacy violations involving students and California schools. PlayOn Sports was found to have violated CCPA opt-out requirements and consumer notice obligations. The case signals the Agency's attention to student data privacy as an enforcement priority.

findings.title: FTC COPPA Rule Amendments Take Effect April 22, 2026 — Enforcement Begins on Expanded Biometric and Government ID Provisions
findings.source: Federal Trade Commission / Taft Privacy & Data Security Insights
findings.summary: The FTC will begin enforcing significant amendments to the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule (COPPA Rule) on April 22, 2026, one year after the finalized amendments were published in the Federal Register on April 22, 2025. The updated COPPA Rule expands the definition of 'personal information' to include biometric identifiers (fingerprints, retina patterns, facial templates, voiceprints), government-issued identifiers (state ID card numbers, birth certificate numbers, passport numbers), and other new categories. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson has publicly committed to aggressive COPPA enforcement as a priority. Civil penalties for violations can exceed $50,000 per violation.

findings.title: CISA Delays Final CIRCIA Cyber Incident Reporting Rule to May 2026 Amid Appropriations Lapse
findings.summary: CISA has pushed the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) to May 2026, citing the need to streamline requirements and reduce industry burden following public comments on the April 2024 proposed rule. However, a lapse in DHS appropriations further delayed scheduled CIRCIA town hall meetings planned for March 9 through April 2, 2026, making additional delays to the final rule likely. When finalized, CIRCIA will require critical infrastructure operators to report substantial cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours and ransomware payments within 24 hours.

findings.title: NIST Releases AI RMF Profile Concept Note on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure
findings.summary: On April 7, 2026, NIST released a concept note for an AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) Profile focused on Trustworthy AI in Critical Infrastructure. The profile is intended to guide critical infrastructure operators toward specific risk management practices when deploying AI-enabled capabilities. This follows NIST's broader AI RMF initiative and the February 2026 launch of the AI Agent Standards Initiative by NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), which addresses autonomous AI agents. The concept note is part of an ongoing effort to develop sector-specific AI governance profiles.

findings.title: NIST Publishes Preliminary Draft Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (NISTIR 8596) for Public Comment
findings.summary: NIST published a preliminary draft of the Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (NISTIR 8596), also called the 'Cyber AI Profile,' on December 16, 2025, with a 45-day public comment period ending January 30, 2026. The profile provides guidelines for using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0) to accelerate secure adoption of AI systems, offering a structured approach to managing cybersecurity risks specific to AI. NIST plans to develop an initial public draft for release in 2026 following comment review. Law firm and industry commentary on the draft began appearing in January 2026.

findings.title: Indiana, Kentucky, and Rhode Island Comprehensive Privacy Laws Take Effect January 1, 2026
findings.summary: Comprehensive consumer data privacy laws in Indiana (IN SB 5), Kentucky (KY HB 15), and Rhode Island (RI HB 7787/SB 2500) took effect January 1, 2026. All three laws largely follow the Virginia CDPA template. Rhode Island's law has notably low applicability thresholds, covering entities processing data of at least 35,000 consumers or 10,000 consumers when more than 20% of revenue derives from personal data sales. These new laws bring the total number of states with active comprehensive privacy laws to approximately 20, covering more than half the U.S. population.

findings.title: California CPPA Imposes $1.35 Million Fine Against Tractor Supply Co. for CCPA Violations
findings.summary: The California Privacy Protection Agency imposed a $1.35 million fine against Tractor Supply Company for violations of the California Consumer Privacy Act. The enforcement action is part of a series of CPPA enforcement actions in 2026 targeting businesses failing to implement adequate opt-out mechanisms and privacy notices required under the CCPA. Additional 2026 CPPA enforcement actions include a $632,500 fine against American Honda Motor Co. and a $345,178 fine against Todd Snyder, Inc. California's CPPA and AG are conducting an active enforcement campaign targeting CCPA compliance failures.
